unemployment-s2.title: Five people in Country Y
unemployment-s2.text: Ana quit her job as a nurse to move closer to her family and is applying for nursing jobs in her new city. Ben ran a printing press for 20 years; the plant replaced its presses with digital machines, and the jobs open near him need computer skills he does not have. Chen was laid off from a car dealership when sales fell during a recession; he is looking for work. Dee retired at 67 and is not looking for work. Eli lost his job a year ago and has stopped looking because he believes no one is hiring.

unemployment-s3.title: Unemployment rates in Country Z over three years

table.caption: Country Z unemployment (percent of the labor force; invented data for practice)

items.q: What is the labor force in Country X, in millions of people?

why.correct: The labor force is the employed plus the unemployed: $150 + 10 = 160$ million. People not in the labor force are not part of it.

mistakes.why: That is only the employed. The labor force also includes the unemployed, people without a job who are looking: $150 + 10$.
That is the adult population. The labor force leaves out the 90 million who are neither working nor looking.

items.q: What is the unemployment rate in Country X?

mistakes.why: You divided by the adult population. The unemployment rate divides by the labor force (employed + unemployed = 160 million).
You divided by the employed. The denominator is the whole labor force: the employed plus the unemployed.

items.q: What is the labor force participation rate in Country X?

mistakes.why: You used only the employed. The labor force is the employed plus the unemployed, 160 million.
That is the share not in the labor force. Participation is the share that is in it: 160 out of 250.

items.q: If the 2 million discouraged workers in the table were counted as unemployed, what would happen to the unemployment rate?
options: It would rise, to about 7.4%
It would fall, because the labor force would be larger
It would stay at 6.25%, because they have no job either way
It would rise, to 8%, because 2 is added to 6

why.correct: Discouraged workers want a job but have stopped looking, so they are not in the labor force. Leaving them out makes the official rate understate joblessness.
options: Right: the unemployed would be 12 and the labor force 162, so $\frac{12}{162} \times 100 \approx 7.4\%$.
The labor force grows by 2, but the unemployed grow by the same 2 from a much smaller base, so the rate rises.
Moving them into the labor force as unemployed changes both the top and the bottom of the fraction.
Rates are not added like that; recompute the fraction $\frac{12}{162}$.

items.q: What type of unemployment does Ben experience?
options: He is not in the labor force
Structural
Frictional
Cyclical

why.correct: Structural unemployment is a mismatch between workers' skills or locations and the jobs on offer, often after technology or the pattern of demand changes.
options: He is out of work and looking, so he is unemployed and in the labor force.
Right: his skills no longer match the jobs available, because technology changed the industry.
Frictional unemployment is time spent searching between jobs a worker is qualified for; Ben lacks the skills the open jobs need.
Cyclical unemployment comes from a fall in spending in a downturn; Ben's job vanished because the technology changed.

items.q: What type of unemployment does Chen experience?
options: Frictional
Seasonal
Cyclical
Structural

why.correct: Cyclical unemployment rises when the economy's total spending and output fall and firms lay off workers.
options: He did not leave to search for a better match; he was laid off when demand fell.
Nothing suggests a regular yearly pattern; the cause is the recession.
Right: he lost his job because spending fell during a recession.
His skills still fit car sales; the jobs disappeared because sales fell, not because his skills became outdated.

items.q: How are Dee and Eli counted in the official statistics?
options: Both are unemployed, because neither has a job
Dee is outside the labor force and Eli is unemployed
Eli is outside the labor force and Dee is unemployed
Both are outside the labor force, so neither counts as unemployed

why.correct: Only people who are jobless, available and actively looking count as unemployed. Retirees and discouraged workers are outside the labor force.
options: Having no job is not enough: an unemployed person must be available and have looked for work recently.
Eli stopped looking, so he is a discouraged worker and is outside the labor force too.
Dee is retired and not looking, so she is not unemployed.
Right: neither is looking for work. Dee is retired and Eli is a discouraged worker.

items.q: Which of these people is counted in the natural rate of unemployment? Select all that apply.
options: Eli
Ana
Chen
Dee

why.correct: Natural rate = frictional + structural, so Ana (frictional) counts, as Ben (structural) would. Cyclical unemployment is not part of it, and people outside the labor force are not unemployed at all.
options: He has stopped looking, so he is a discouraged worker outside the labor force, not unemployed.
Right: her search after moving is frictional unemployment, part of the natural rate.
His job loss in a recession is cyclical, which is not part of the natural rate.
She is retired and outside the labor force, so she is not unemployed at all.

items.q: What is Country Z's natural rate of unemployment?

why.correct: Natural rate = frictional + structural $= 2.0 + 3.0 = 5.0\%$. It is the same in every year of the table.

mistakes.why: That is the actual rate in Year 2. The natural rate adds only frictional and structural unemployment.
That is only frictional unemployment. Add structural unemployment too: $2 + 3$.

items.q: What is the cyclical unemployment rate in Year 2?

why.correct: Cyclical = actual - natural $= 8.0 - 5.0 = 3.0\%$. Actual = natural + cyclical.

mistakes.why: You added the actual and natural rates. Cyclical unemployment is the actual rate minus the natural rate.
You subtracted only the frictional rate. Subtract the whole natural rate, frictional plus structural: $8 - 5$.

items.q: In Year 3 the actual unemployment rate (4.5%) is below the natural rate. What does that mean?
options: Cyclical unemployment is negative; output is beyond full employment
Frictional unemployment has disappeared
The data contain an error: the actual rate can't be below the natural rate
The economy is in a recession

why.correct: Cyclical unemployment is the actual rate minus the natural rate; it is negative when the economy runs hot and positive in a downturn.
options: Right: $4.5 - 5.0 = -0.5$. Workers are scarce, so output is above its sustainable level for now.
The table still shows 2.0% frictional unemployment in Year 3.
The actual rate can fall below the natural rate for a while when the economy is booming.
In a recession cyclical unemployment is positive, so the actual rate is above the natural rate.

items.q: In which year of the table is Country Z at full employment?
options: No year, because unemployment is above zero in each
Year 1
Year 2
Year 3

why.correct: Full employment is when the actual unemployment rate equals the natural rate: some frictional and structural unemployment remains.
options: Full employment means zero cyclical unemployment, not zero unemployment.
Right: the actual rate equals the natural rate (5.0%), so cyclical unemployment is zero.
At 8.0% the actual rate is above the natural rate, so there is cyclical unemployment.
At 4.5% the actual rate is below the natural rate, beyond full employment.

items.q: Country W has high cyclical unemployment: many willing workers cannot find jobs. Mark a point on its production possibilities curve graph that shows where it is producing.

why.correct: Unemployed workers are resources left idle, so the economy produces inside its PPC: less of both goods than it could.

items.q: Over ten years, many more adults in Country W join the labor force, and they find jobs. Show the effect on Country W's production possibilities curve.

why.correct: More labor is more of a factor of production, so the economy can make more of both goods: the PPC shifts out.

slips.PPC: More workers is more of a factor of production: the curve moves out, not in.

items.q: Which statement about the natural rate of unemployment is correct?
options: It is the sum of frictional and cyclical unemployment
It is one fixed number, the same in each country
It is the unemployment rate when cyclical unemployment is zero
It is an unemployment rate of zero percent

why.correct: Natural rate = frictional + structural. When the actual rate equals it, the economy is at full employment.
options: The natural rate is frictional plus structural; cyclical unemployment is the part above it.
It differs across countries and can change over time with job search tools, training and labor laws.
Right: at the natural rate only frictional and structural unemployment remain.
People are always changing jobs and retraining, so some unemployment remains at full employment.

items.q: Ivy works 10 hours a week at a store but wants full-time work. How does the way she is counted affect the unemployment rate as a measure of joblessness?
options: She counts as unemployed, so the rate overstates joblessness
She counts as outside the labor force, so the rate is unaffected
She counts as half employed and half unemployed
She counts as employed, so the rate understates unused labor

why.correct: Underemployed and discouraged workers both make the official unemployment rate a low reading of how much labor goes unused.
options: Anyone with paid work in the survey week counts as employed, even part-time.
She has a job, so she is in the labor force as employed.
The survey has no half categories: she is employed.
Right: part-time workers who want full-time jobs are underemployed but counted as employed.

items.q: One spring, 3 million students finish school in Country V and start looking for work; no one loses a job. What happens to the unemployment rate right away?
options: It rises, because new job seekers enter the labor force as unemployed
It falls, because the labor force grows
It stays the same, because no one was laid off
It rises, because the graduates were counted as employed while in school

why.correct: The unemployment rate depends on who is looking, not just on layoffs. New entrants searching for work add to frictional unemployment.
options: Right: the graduates are now available and looking, so they join the labor force as unemployed until they find jobs.
The labor force grows, but by people who are all unemployed, so the share unemployed rises.
Unemployment can rise without layoffs when new searchers enter the labor force.
Full-time students not looking for work are outside the labor force, not employed.

items.q: Country V's labor force is 80 million and its unemployment rate is 5%. How many people are unemployed, in millions?

mistakes.why: You multiplied 5 by 80 but did not divide by 100. Five percent is 0.05, so $0.05 \times 80 = 4$.
You divided 80 by 5. Five percent of 80 is $0.05 \times 80$.
